Articles were deduplicated 356 using DOI and normalized title information, with screening prepared in the R package

Eligibility, Study Selection, and Effect-Size Selection

We applied cumulative eligibility criteria during abstract screening, full-text review, and data extraction. Because comparative optimism is event-specific, we restricted inclusion to perceived risk of COVID-19 infection and excluded studies that assessed or averaged across other outcomes, such as disease severity or mortality. Studies had to assess comparative optimism through a direct self-other comparison or separate estimates of personal risk and the risk of a comparison target. As comparisons with close others (e.g., friends) strongly reduce comparative optimism, we excluded such comparisons while retaining comparisons with an average other (Helweg-Larsen & Shepperd, 2001; Zakay, 1996). For articles identified through the additional OpenAlex search, we did not require abstracts to explicitly describe a self-other comparison, as some studies were framed in terms of risk perception. Articles were excluded at abstract screening only when they clearly failed to meet the eligibility criteria, for example, by assessing exclusively noncomparative risk perception or using measures unsuitable for assessing comparative optimism. When eligibility remained unclear, articles were retained for full-text review. Eligible scales had at least five response options and permitted calculation of a standardized effect size. Direct measures also required a midpoint. Furthermore, samples had to include at least 30 participants and comparative optimism had to be measured in the same questionnaire in which the focal COVID-19 event was presented. Inclusion was restricted to adults from the general population who had not been selected on the basis of clinical status. To avoid manipulation-induced shifts in risk perception, we excluded comparative optimism assessed after interventions, while retaining control and inert or neutral conditions. Because anonymity can affect effect sizes, anonymous recruitment was required and telephone interviews were excluded (Sweldens et al., 2014).

At full-text review, reports had to be accessible and describe the comparative optimism measure. We included data collected between January 1, 2020, and December 31, 2021. Later data were excluded because too few eligible samples were available for a separate analysis, and by the end of 2021 vaccines were widely available in many countries (Mathieu et al., 2021). In addition, vaccination rates differed substantially across countries (Pilkington et al., 2022), and comparative optimism varied across pandemic phases (Izydorczak et al., 2022; Lyu et al., 2025; McColl et al., 2022). Because vaccination changes infection rates and the perceived controllability of an infection, both of which are associated with comparative optimism (Chambers et al., 2003; Klein & Helweg-Larsen, 2002), we excluded participants known to be vaccinated where vaccination status was available, and we modeled collection period (2020 versus 2021) as a moderator, without interactions to keep the number of estimated coefficients as small as necessary. Depending on available variables, we also excluded invalid risk responses and, in relevant datasets, participants with known prior infection, ineligible age, failed attention checks, or exposure to manipulated conditions. When studies reported multiple eligible infection-risk estimates, we prioritized a one-year time horizon and otherwise selected the estimate closest to one year. The one-year time horizon was the most common version and represented a compromise, given that some studies did not report a time horizon.

We sought both individual participant data (IPD) and aggregate data (AD). Because nationality was modeled as a random effect, data had to be available separately by nationality.

We screened eligible studies for openly available IPD and contacted authors when these data were unavailable. When IPD could not be obtained, studies remained eligible when sufficient aggregate statistics were reported to calculate a standardized effect size. We included one effect size per sample from a single measurement occasion. In longitudinal datasets, one eligible wave was selected using a reproducible fixed seed. Other datasets contributed the first eligible occasion or distinct replication cohorts, as documented in the scripts on OSF (https://osf.io/hpwut/). Distinct national samples contributed separate effects, whereas duplicate reports of the same participant data were counted once. Detailed eligibility and effect-selection rules appear in Supplemental Material Section S1.2.

Quality Assessment

We used a targeted, domain-specific checklist rather than a generic risk-of-bias tool because designs varied and comparative optimism was a primary outcome in some studies and a secondary outcome in others. Given known measurement flexibilities and potential artifacts (Harris & Hahn, 2011), we evaluated (a) conceptual clarity, (b) measurement choices, (c) reporting and transparency, and (d) open-science practices. Eighteen items were coded not addressed, fully addressed, or partly addressed where a predefined intermediate category was meaningful. We applied the partly addressed category generously and, when a case could reasonably receive either of two ratings, assigned the more favorable rating. For example, a choice of direct or indirect measurement was fully addressed when authors explained that choice while considering the alternative. Giving a methodological reason without considering the alternative was partly addressed. Merely stating which measure was used was not addressed. Statistical artifacts were partly addressed when authors identified a relevant artifact but did not examine its implications. They were fully addressed when authors assessed or controlled for the artifact, or explained why it did not apply. Where no meaningful partial condition existed, such as for public data availability, we used only fully addressed and not addressed. Given the sensitivity of summary scores to item selection and weighting (Ahn et al., 2023; Losilla et al., 2018), we did not calculate a total score, exclude studies on the basis of checklist ratings, or use a score as a moderator. Moreover, as aggregating multiple quality indicators requires an appropriate measurement basis (Scherer & Emslander, 2025), the checklist was only used descriptively. The full checklist and coding anchors are provided in Section S2 and Table S3 of the Supplemental Material. Below, we report how many reports received each rating for each checklist item.

Data Handling

Below, we describe how we operationalized the primary outcome, followed by the selection and coding of moderators at the IPD (participant) and study levels, including how we handled known influential factors that were not the primary focus.

Primary Outcome

The primary outcome was comparative optimism for the likelihood of getting infected with COVID-19. To ensure comparability across effects, we set a common reference point of 0 (equal perceived risk). For indirect measures, we subtracted each participant's own-risk judgment from the comparison target's risk judgment. For direct measures, we subtracted the comparative midpoint from each response after aligning the scoring direction. All measures were coded so that positive comparative scores indicated lower perceived risk for the self than for the comparison target (comparatively optimistic responses), negative scores indicated higher perceived risk (comparatively pessimistic responses), and zero indicated equal perceived risk. Note that these labels describe responses, not individuals or the objective accuracy of their judgments. We then estimated comparative optimism as Cohen's d for each sample in the average-effect analysis. When IPD were available, we computed d directly from raw scores; otherwise, we used reported one-sample (direct) or paired-samples (indirect) tests, or derived d from descriptive statistics or confidence intervals using standard transformations (Cohen, 1988 (Cohen, /2013;; Lakens, 2013). These procedures are detailed in Supplemental Material Section S3. For raw mean differences, Cohen's d was computed as follows:

A positive value indicates that the sample mean was above the equal-risk reference in sample standard deviation units. It does not indicate the proportion of responses indicating lower perceived risk for the self than for others. The corresponding standard error (SE) was estimated following Borenstein et al. (2009) for a one-sample or paired-sample t test.

𝑆𝐸 = 1 𝑁 + 𝑑 2𝑁

To enable IPD-level analyses, we standardized comparative scores within each dataset by dividing each participant's score by the full eligible sample standard deviation without mean-centering, thereby preserving 0 as the equal-risk reference. The mean of these standardized scores equals Cohen's d.

Selection and Coding of Moderators

Individual-Level Moderators. Within each IPD sample, age, gender, and education were examined in separate unadjusted regressions. Age was centered within the sample with available age data, and its coefficient represents the change associated with one additional year. Nonpositive or nonfinite age values were treated as unavailable. Gender was coded female = 0 and male = 1, so its coefficient represents the difference in standardized comparative scores between male and female participants. Other or unavailable responses were omitted only from the gender analysis and remained eligible for analyses that did not require gender.

Education distinguished bachelor's degree or higher from below bachelor's degree, with the latter as the reference; its coefficient therefore represents bachelor's degree or higher minus lower education. Categories were mapped from the available questionnaires, codebooks, variable labels, and publications. No demographic values were imputed. Samples contributed to a moderator analysis only when the predictor varied.

Study-Level Moderators. Of particular interest were associations of measurement format and response-scale length with comparative optimism effect sizes, as proposed by egocentrism theory and statistical artifact theory (Chambers et al., 2003; Harris & Hahn, 2011). Measurement format was coded as direct or indirect. Response-scale length was represented by 5, 7, 11, or 101 response options, and planned adjacent contrasts compared 5 with 7, 7 with 11, and 11 with 101 options. Comparison targets were classified as specific when the comparison person was personally matched, for example by age, gender, or wording such as "someone like you". Other comparison targets were classified as unspecific. The comparison-target coefficient represents unspecific minus specific targets.

In addition, we compared student and nonstudent samples, with student population effect-coded so that its coefficient represents students minus nonstudents. National collectivism was represented by the continuous Global Collectivism Index (GCI; Pelham et al., 2022), with higher values indicating greater collectivism. Published units were retained and GCI was modeled linearly. Collection period was coded dichotomously as 2020 or 2021 based on the end of data collection, with 2020 as the reference; its coefficient therefore represents 2021 minus 2020. Where the day was unknown, day 28 was used to assign the period. For the extended demographic model, mean age was entered in years and the proportion of female participants on a 0 to 1 scale. Effects missing either sample mean age or the proportion of female participants were omitted from the extended demographic model.

Analytical Strategy

We used a two-step IPD approach. In step one, IPD from each study were used to estimate a sample-specific effect size; in step two, these effects were synthesized in a metaanalysis. This strategy allowed us to combine effects derived from IPD with those calculated from aggregate data. We also examined individual-level moderators by estimating within-study regressions and then meta-analyzing the resulting regression coefficients for standardized comparative scores (Van Aert, 2022).

We estimated the average effect and heterogeneity using a multilevel model for the nested and partially crossed data structure (Assink & Wibbelink, 2016; Cheung, 2019). To estimate the fixed and random effects, we used the metafor package (Viechtbauer, 2010) in R (R Core Team, 2022). Although the design is highly unbalanced, simulation work suggests that variance-component estimation and inference in such models are still more accurate than ignoring the crossed structure (Fernández-Castilla et al., 2020).

Descriptive Analyses

We summarized measurement format, response-scale length, population, nationality, and collection period. For each combination of measurement format and original scale length, we reported the numbers of effects, studies, and articles and the summed available sample sizes. For the available IPD, we described responses indicating lower, equal, or higher perceived risk for the self than for others, separately by measurement format and original scale length. For IPD samples with 3 to 5,000 observations, Shapiro-Wilk tests were calculated as exploratory normality diagnostics; they did not determine model selection, study eligibility, or effect exclusion.

Main Analysis

The unconditional model was specified as follows. We fitted a multilevel model with studies nested within articles and nationality effects crossed with this hierarchy, using random intercepts for study, article, and nationality. The model was estimated by restricted maximum likelihood (REML). The observations in this meta-analytic model were sample-level effect estimates. We report the pooled mean with a 95% confidence interval and a 95% prediction interval based on the total random-effects variance (Riley et al., 2011). Heterogeneity was summarized by the estimated variance components (τ²), their standard deviations (τ), profile-likelihood confidence intervals, and approximate I² values. We used likelihood-ratio tests based on maximum likelihood estimation to compare the full model with reduced models omitting one random component, and retained the full crossed random-effects structure in subsequent models. Fixed-effect inference used model-based t and F tests with containment degrees of freedom as implemented in metafor (Viechtbauer, 2010). All tests were two-sided, and α = .05 was used as a conventional descriptive reference rather than as a confirmatory decision threshold.

Moderator Analysis

To examine between-sample moderators, we fitted a mixed-effects meta-regression with the same random-effects structure. Measurement format and response-scale length were entered simultaneously as additive methodological moderators. Student population, national collectivism, collection period, and comparison-target specificity were included in the same model. To examine the changes resulting from adding the proportion of female participants and average age of the sample, we compared three models. Model 1 was the primary model.

Model 2 retained the same predictors but excluded effects without sample mean age or female proportion. Model 3 used the same effects as Model 2 and added these two predictors.

All categorical moderators were coded so that model coefficients represented the specified comparisons. We report ordinary 95% confidence intervals and unadjusted p values.

We did not apply a multiplicity correction because the analyses were explicitly exploratory and were intended to identify patterns for further investigation rather than to provide confirmatory tests of a prespecified hypothesis family. To describe the extent to which the moderators accounted for heterogeneity, we compared the variance components and approximate I² values of the unconditional and additive moderator models fitted to the same effects. We calculated the proportional change in each variance component and in their sum.

Overall model fit was compared using a likelihood-ratio test after refitting both models with maximum likelihood. Changes in heterogeneity were interpreted descriptively.

For each individual-level moderator, we synthesized the within-sample coefficients using their squared standard errors as sampling variances, REML estimation, containment inference, and the same crossed random-intercept structure for study, article, and nationality.

In additional exploratory meta-regressions, each set of within-sample coefficients was regressed on the corresponding sample composition variable and on measurement format, response-scale length, student population, and national collectivism. The corresponding composition variables were mean age for age coefficients, proportion female for gender coefficients, and proportion below a bachelor's degree for education coefficients.

Sensitivity Analyses and Small-Study Effects

We assessed robustness by omitting all effects from one article at a time and refitting both the unconditional model and the primary additive moderator model. We also used studentized residuals from the unconditional model to flag effects with |z| > 1.96 as potential, rather than definitive, outliers (Viechtbauer & Cheung, 2010). This cutoff approximates the conventional two-sided 5% normal threshold and was used only to probe sensitivity, not to determine eligibility. We then refitted the unconditional, primary moderator, and extended demographic models without the flagged effects, while retaining all effects in the analyses of record.

For examining small-study and selection effects, we first inspected a funnel plot for asymmetry (Renkewitz & Keiner, 2019; Sterne et al., 2011). Small-study effects were then examined in a multilevel meta-regression with 1/√N as the predictor and the same crossed random-intercept structure used in the primary models (Rodgers & Pustejovsky, 2021). A positive coefficient indicates larger estimated effects in smaller samples under the fitted model. However, this association does not by itself establish publication bias or provide a corrected pooled effect. As a complementary selection-model analysis, we applied Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis (RoBMA; Maier et al., 2022) using RoBMA version 3.6.0 (Bartoš & Maier, 2020). Because RoBMA requires independent inputs, multiple effects within each study were combined into one inverse-variance-weighted study estimate. The alternativeeffect prior was Normal (0, 1), and the alternative heterogeneity prior was inverse-gamma with shape 1 and scale 0.15; the corresponding null models fixed the effect or heterogeneity at 0. The selection component used a cumulative two-sided weight function with p-value cutpoints of .001 and .05 and Dirichlet parameters α = (1, 1, 1). In plain terms, the three selection weights each have the same expected value before the data are considered, although the model allows them to differ. Prior model probabilities were .50 for the presence versus absence of an effect, heterogeneity, and selection. Models were averaged across these components. Because the required aggregation does not preserve the crossed article and nationality structure of the primary models, the RoBMA results were treated as complementary.

Results

Literature Search Figure 1 Flow Chart Note. The flow chart is adapted from the PRISMA template (Page et al., 2022). Only peerreviewed journal articles and preprints that were published after 2019 were included. The database searches identified 498 records, with 79 from Web of Science Core Collection, 52 from APA PsycINFO, and 367 from OpenAlex. After deduplication, 373 records remained for title and abstract screening, of which 261 were excluded (see Figure 1).

The remaining 112 reports advanced to full-text review, and 64 were excluded at that stage.

Of the 48 reports that met the inclusion criteria, 10 were excluded at the data-availability or extraction stage. Thus, 38 articles were included in the analysis. These articles reported 50 studies and contributed 135 sample-level effect estimates across 55 nationalities (summed effect-level N = 88,935, not an established count of unique participants). Individual participant data were available for 123 effects from 38 studies reported in 28 articles (summed effect-level N = 79,902); for the remaining 12 effects, only aggregate data were available (summed effect-level N = 9,033). Exclusion reasons are detailed in Supplemental Material Section S1.3 (Table S2). All 135 effects were included in the pooled analysis. One effect, based on a 9-option response scale, was also retained in the response descriptives and selection-model analysis but excluded from the moderator regressions because the planned adjacent scale contrasts represented 5, 7, 11, and 101 response options. Accordingly, the primary moderator analysis included 134 effects from 49 studies reported in 38 articles.

Descriptives

Effect-level sample sizes ranged from 30 to 4,313, with a mean of 658.78 and a median of 499. Across effects with available demographic information, the sample mean age averaged 37.03 years across 126 effects, SD = 9.06, and the proportion of female participants averaged 54.24% across 134 effects, SD = 13.01 percentage points. These values are unweighted descriptions of effect-level characteristics. Of the 135 effects, 23 used direct and 112 used indirect measures. Most effects came from nonstudent samples (n = 115) and used unspecific comparison targets (n = 94). Scale lengths ranged from 5 to 101 options, with 101option scales most common (n = 71). Recruitment ended during 2020 for 113 effects and and 12,900, or 16.14%, indicated higher perceived risk for the self. The distributions varied 651 substantially across measurement formats and scale lengths (see

Table 2). Additional 652 descriptive breakdowns and normality diagnostics appear in Supplemental Material Section 653 S4. Sample-level comparative-score distributions are available on OSF (https://osf.io/hpwut/). 654

Main Analysis

The crossed random-intercept meta-analysis of all 135 effects indicated positive comparative optimism on average, d = 0.334, SE = 0.054, 95% CI [0.225, 0.444], t(37) = 6.18, p < .001. The 95% prediction interval ranged from -0.371 to 1.040. Thus, the positive pooled mean coexisted with a range of plausible true effects that included comparative pessimism. Heterogeneity was substantial, Q(134) = 7,741.65, p < .001, with an approximate total I² of 95.68%. The remaining approximately 4.32% is the sampling-variance component of the model's total variation. Variance components for study, article, and nationality were 0.00685, 0.07213, and 0.03924, respectively (τ = 0.083, 0.269, and 0.198).

The approximate shares of total variation were 5.55%, 58.37%, and 31.76%, respectively. Profile-likelihood 95% confidence intervals for τ were [0.208, 0.351] for article and [0.164, 0.244] for nationality. The study-level lower limit was 0.046, but the upper profile bound did not converge and is therefore not reported. Likelihood-ratio tests supported retaining each random component; all ps < .001. A caterpillar plot of the sample-level effects, their confidence intervals, the pooled estimate and its confidence interval, and the prediction interval is presented in Figure 2. The effect sizes and sample characteristics for all 135 effects are presented in Table 4. One effect from Yang and Dang (2026) and three national estimates from de Castro et al. (2025) had absolute studentized residuals greater than 1.96. Excluding all four increased the pooled estimate to d = 0.356, 95% CI [0.257, 0.454], p < .001. The three de Castro et al.

effects used direct measures with 11 response options, so their exclusion also changed the composition of the measurement-format × scale-length groups in the moderator analyses (Supplemental Table S9). In a separate leave-one-article-out analysis, the pooled estimate remained positive across all 38 refits. It ranged from d = 0.312 when Izydorczak et al. (2023) was omitted to d = 0.372 when de Castro et al. (2025) was omitted, changes of -0.022 and +0.038 from the full-data estimate of d = 0.334, respectively (Supplemental Table S8). Study-Level Moderator Analyses

The primary additive moderator model (Model 1), which includes 134 effects after excluding the 9-option sample, is summarized in Table 5 alongside its complete-case and demographic extensions. The joint moderator test yielded F(8, 29) = 3.02, p = .014, although residual heterogeneity remained substantial, QE(125) = 4,032.72, p < .001. Relative to an unconditional model fitted to the same 134 effects, the sum of the random-effect variances decreased from 0.11823 to 0.10239, a descriptive reduction of 13.40%, while approximate total I² decreased from 95.66% to 95.02%. A maximum-likelihood comparison also favored the moderator model, χ²(8) = 22.54, p = .004. Direct measures yielded smaller adjusted effects than indirect measures, b = -0.359, SE = 0.125, 95% CI [-0.616, -0.103], p = .008. All three adjacent scale contrasts were negative, but neither the individual contrasts nor their joint test was statistically significant (Table 5). The results therefore did not establish a monotonic attenuation of comparative optimism with increasing response options. Recruitment during 2021 was associated with a larger adjusted effect than recruitment during 2020, b = 0.153, 95% CI [0.012, 0.295], p = .034. National collectivism showed a positive but imprecise association, b = 0.071 per GCI point, 95% CI [-0.001, 0.143], p = .054. Student versus nonstudent samples and unspecific versus specific comparison targets showed no clear adjusted differences, ps = .695 and .796.

The direction of the measurement-format coefficient remained negative in all 38 leave-one-article-out analyses and had p < .05 in 37. None of the three scale contrasts had p < .05 in any article-omission fit. After the four flagged effects were excluded, the direct-minusindirect coefficient remained negative, b = -0.306, p = .012, while the three scale contrasts and their joint test remained above .05, F(3, 29) = 2.21, p = .109. The 2021 coefficient was more sensitive because 16 of the 22 effects from 2021 came from one article. Omitting that article changed the estimate to b = -0.072, p = .445.11-versus-7 contrast remained negative, b = -0.328, p = .019, but the joint scale test remained nonsignificant, F(3, 18) = 3.01, p = .057.

Individual Participant Data Moderator Analyses

The pooled within-sample age association was b = -0.00223 standardized comparative-score units per year, 95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00041], p = .094, based on 117 effects. The male-minus-female association was b = 0.026, 95% CI [-0.037, 0.089], p = .402, based on 122 effects. The association for a bachelor's degree or higher versus lower education was b = -0.006, 95% CI [-0.107, 0.095], p = .891, based on 17 effects from eight articles. All three confidence intervals included zero, with substantially less evidence available for education. The complete sample-specific coefficient estimates and confidence intervals are presented in separate forest plots for age, gender, and education in Figures S1-S3 of the Supplemental Material.

Exploratory meta-regressions then examined variation in these within-sample coefficients. Analysis details are in Supplemental Material Section S5. For age, the joint moderator test was F(7, 16) = 2.96, p = .034. Mean sample age was positively associated with the age coefficient, b = 0.000230 per year, 95% CI [0.000010, 0.000449], p = .040; the remaining moderator coefficients had ps ≥ .087. For gender, the joint moderator test was F(7, 20) = 1.83, p = .136. The proportion of female participants was positively associated with the male-minus-female coefficient, b = 0.263 per full-unit difference in female proportion, 95% CI [0.066, 0.461], p = .009, whereas the remaining moderator coefficients had ps ≥ .155. The education-coefficient meta-regression was based on 17 effects, and its joint moderator test had only one denominator degree of freedom, F(7, 1) = 3.68, p = .382. The limited denominator degrees of freedom constrain interpretation. Full coefficient tables for the age, gender, and education meta-regressions are provided in Supplemental Tables S5-S7.

Small-Study Effects and Selection Models

The distribution of the sample-level effect estimates in relation to their standard errors is shown in Figure 3. The multilevel small-study regression included 134 effects, excluding the 9-option sample, and indicated that smaller samples tended to yield larger effects, b = 1.074 for 1/√N, SE = 0.492, 95% CI [0.100, 2.048], p = .031. This association does not distinguish selective reporting from design differences or other confounding and should not be interpreted as a bias-corrected effect estimate. Discussion

This study aimed to determine whether comparative optimism was observed for COVID-19 infection risk and to identify factors that might account for variation in the effect. Particular attention was given to measurement characteristics in both the meta-analysis and the quality assessment. In the following, we discuss these findings, their methodological implications, and what they may mean for future research.

The Average Effect of Comparative Optimism

Across 135 effect estimates from 50 studies reported in 38 articles, comparative optimism for COVID-19 infection risk was observed on average, with a pooled effect of d = 0.334, 95% CI [0.225, 0.444]. The pooled estimate remained positive in every leave-onearticle-out analysis and changed only slightly after the four effects flagged by the residual criterion were omitted. At the same time, the prediction interval ranged from -0.371 to 1.040, indicating that effects could range from comparative pessimism to pronounced optimism across the settings represented in the analysis. Heterogeneity remained high despite the restriction to a single event and the additional inclusion criteria. Furthermore, effect sizes increased as sample size decreased in the multilevel analysis, and RoBMA strongly favored models that included a selection component. The model-averaged RoBMA estimate was somewhat smaller than the pooled effect but remained clearly positive. Because RoBMA did not represent the article-and nationality-level dependencies of the primary model, its results complement rather than replace the multilevel estimate.

The individual participant data show how responses were distributed across respondents. Across the available IPD, 47.75% of participants reported lower personal risk than the comparison target, 36.11% reported equal risk, and 16.14% reported higher personal risk. Responses indicating lower personal risk were thus nearly three times as common as responses indicating higher personal risk, in line with the positive pooled effect. The large proportion of equal-risk responses is not visible in the average. Izydorczak et al. (2023) argued that the absence of a comparative difference may represent a meaningful response category rather than merely the midpoint of a continuous optimism-pessimism dimension.

Taken together, these results indicate that people on average judged their own risk of COVID-19 infection to be lower than that of others, but that the magnitude of this difference, and in some settings its direction, varied substantially across articles and countries. The smallstudy pattern and the selection component suggest that the pooled estimate may modestly overstate the average effect in the full evidence base. Comparative optimism is therefore best understood as a typical tendency rather than a stable effect of fixed size. The pooled effect reflects a shift in the balance of responses rather than a uniform response pattern, and it combines how many participants respond optimistically with how strongly they do so. The distribution does not show whether judgments were objectively accurate or which process produced them, since egocentrism, motivational processes, statistical artifacts, and differences in how comparison targets were understood may all contribute. Whether equal-risk responses identify a qualitatively distinct group, reflect limited scale resolution, or both, and whether strongly influenced by event severity. The findings therefore do not establish that either format is more valid, and it remains unclear whether the difference observed in the present analysis reflects measurement format itself, characteristics of the contributing studies, or event-related factors that were not represented in the analysis. The observed direction is also compatible with statistical artifact theory, which allows the two formats to be affected differently by measurement artifacts such as scale attenuation and base rate regression (Harris & Hahn, 2011). However, the present study did not directly assess base rate regression and therefore cannot distinguish between these explanations. The 23 direct effects came from only 13 articles, and all 10 negative direct estimates came from three of them, so the format difference may partly reflect a small number of articles. In sum, the size of comparative optimism depends on how it is measured, and because 112 of the 135 effects came from indirect measures, the pooled estimate mostly rests on indirect measurement. Nevertheless, in contrast to that earlier synthesis, we observed a consistent association with measurement format within a single event, although, as discussed below, the present analysis cannot establish that the single-event focus accounts for this difference.

Scale attenuation, one of the measurement artifacts discussed above, was examined more directly through the response-scale contrasts. As outlined in the theoretical background, bounded response scales can restrict the representation of comparative judgments, with fewer response options potentially producing greater attenuation and affecting comparativeoptimism estimates (Harris & Hahn, 2011). Although all three adjacent contrasts in the primary additive model were negative, as expected under scale attenuation, neither the individual contrasts nor their joint test was statistically significant. The primary analysis therefore did not establish a systematic reduction in comparative optimism with increasing scale length.

In the secondary complete-case and extended demographic models, the 11-versus-7 contrast was negative and statistically significant. The joint scale test was also significant when the primary model was restricted to effects with complete demographic information, but not when mean age and female proportion were added as predictors. These findings provide some evidence consistent with scale attenuation, although they appeared only in reduced evidence sets. Across all three models, the decline was most pronounced between 7 and 11 options, whereas the contrast between 11 and 101 options was close to zero. Scale attenuation can therefore neither be confirmed nor excluded. If it operates, it appears to matter mainly for scales shorter than 11 options, but scale length and measurement format are partly confounded, so the present data cannot separate their influence.

For comparison-target specificity, we found no clear difference between unspecific and specific targets. This does not correspond to findings suggesting that target characteristics can affect comparative optimism (Kulesza et al., 2023). Targets also differed in wording and event time horizons that could not be coded consistently, so this finding does not establish that target characteristics are irrelevant. Larger differences between targets, such as comparisons with close rather than unknown others, may still influence comparative judgments (Helweg-Larsen & Shepperd, 2001; Price et al., 2006; Zakay, 1996).

Beyond the measurement-related moderators, we also considered country-level, temporal, and sample characteristics. Previous cross-cultural studies have reported different comparative-optimism patterns in Western and East Asian samples, although the direction can depend on the comparison target and design (Chang & Asakawa, 2003; Heine & Lehman, 1995). The association with the Global Collectivism Index was positive in all three models, meaning that comparative optimism was larger, not smaller, in more collectivistic countries, which runs counter to the expectation of weaker optimistic bias in collectivistic cultures. The confidence interval excluded zero only in the model that also included sample mean age and female proportion and in the one leave-one-article-out analysis that omitted de Castro et al. (2025). Thus, the strength of the evidence depended on the model specification and on a single article. Differences between countries may also reflect other contextual variables. Yang and Dang (2026), for example, reported no difference between collectivistic and individualistic countries but found larger comparative differences in countries with greater income inequality, primarily because perceived risk for others was higher. Because we did not account for differences in governmental restrictions or COVID-19 incidence across countries, the pattern can also reflect differences in these factors.

Effects were larger for samples whose data collection ended in 2021 than in 2020 in all three models. This pattern is difficult to interpret alongside reports of both increasing and decreasing comparative optimism over time, including the decrease reported by Lyu et al. (2025). Both egocentrism and statistical-artifact accounts relate comparative optimism to event base rates (Chambers et al., 2003; Harris et al., 2017). To the extent that infection became more likely over the relevant time horizon, we would therefore have expected smaller rather than larger effects. However, calendar year does not establish that infection risk increased comparably across the sampled settings or that participants perceived such an increase. Moreover, the 22 effects from 2021 came from only five articles, 16 of them from one; omitting that article from the primary moderator analysis changed the estimate to a small negative value. Given its dependence on a single article and unmeasured differences in incidence, restrictions, and vaccination, the period contrast cannot be interpreted as a general temporal trend or attributed to a specific pandemic development.

Samples with a higher proportion of women showed slightly smaller comparative optimism effects in the extended model. Yet the individual participant data did not provide clear evidence that women reported less comparative optimism than men within the same samples. This is in line with earlier COVID-19 studies, which reported greater optimism among men in some assessments and no gender differences in others (Doliński et al., 2020; Hoorens et al., 2022; Vieites et al., 2021). The smaller effects in samples with more women may therefore reflect other characteristics of those samples rather than a difference between women and men. In an exploratory second-stage analysis of the within-sample coefficients, the male-minus-female difference was larger in samples with more women (b = 0.263, p = .009; Supplemental Table S6). Men therefore reported relatively more comparative optimism than women as the proportion of women rose. Because the joint moderator test was not significant, this pattern is preliminary, but it suggests that the pooled gender coefficient may mask differences related to sample composition.

Neither the between-sample nor the individual-level age analysis provided clear

evidence of an association, and the individual-level education estimate likewise included zero, based on only 17 effects from eight articles. Earlier studies reported higher optimism about infection risk among older individuals, partly in interaction with gender (Attema et al., 2021; Hoorens et al., 2022), which our separate, unadjusted analyses of age and gender could not examine. Student and nonstudent samples did not differ clearly, so there was no clear evidence that the pooled estimate depends on sample type.

Taken together, the moderator results differ in how much they rest on a few articles.

The format direction held in every omission analysis, whereas the period and collectivism associations and the significance of the 11-versus-7 contrast depended on the contributing articles or on the model specification. Several moderator results may therefore partly reflect a small number of articles with extreme estimates, and they are best treated as hypotheses for future syntheses with more balanced evidence across measurement formats, scale lengths, and periods.

Heterogeneity, Quality, and Consequences

Although the joint moderator model improved model fit, it reduced the sum of the estimated heterogeneity variances by only 13.40%, and most variation between effect sizes remained unexplained. As shown in Figure 3, considerable variation was also present among larger samples, where sampling error is smaller, so the heterogeneity is not merely sampling noise in small studies. Most of the variation lay between articles, which points to article-level features such as item wording and time horizons that could not be coded consistently. The substantial remaining heterogeneity shows that restricting the synthesis to a single event did not isolate measurement influences, and the present analysis cannot establish that removing between-event variation accounts for the difference from the earlier synthesis across events (see Sweldens et al., 2014). This variation may also contribute to the mixed findings regarding the consequences of comparative optimism. Associations with protective behavior have been inconsistent (Cho et al., 2013; Shepperd et al., 2017; Taylor et al., 1992). Studies identified in our search linked higher comparative optimism to lower psychological distress (Doliński et al., 2020; Hua et al., 2023). Other studies linked it to lower perceived severity, information seeking, or adherence to protective recommendations (Ju & Downey, 2025; Park et al., 2021), whereas null or positive associations with protective behavior were also reported (De Witte et al., 2023; Nordfjærn et al., 2021; Sætrevik & Bjørkheim, 2022; Wolaver & Doces, 2022). Vaccination findings were similarly mixed, with several studies finding no negative association (Holt et al., 2022; Salvador-Casara et al., 2022; Wolff, 2021). Whether the heterogeneity in measurement and context found here contributes to these mixed findings could not be tested, because the present synthesis did not examine these outcomes.

Our quality assessment also raises concerns about how measurement choices were reported. Measurement format, comparison target, and response scale were rarely justified on empirical grounds. Only a few articles justified the measurement format in any way, and none fully justified the response scale. Statistical artifact theory was explicitly addressed by only one of the included articles (Vieites et al., 2021). That article addressed scale attenuation only by using seven instead of five response options, which remains susceptible to it. The theory describes several mechanisms through which measurement and sampling can influence comparative-optimism estimates. Limited consideration of these factors makes it difficult to determine whether differences between studies reflect substantive variation in comparative optimism, methodological differences between studies, or both.

Recommendations

Although the findings do not identify a universally preferable measurement format or scale length, they support several recommendations for transparent measurement and reporting. We encourage standardized, empirically grounded approaches to measuring comparative optimism, supported by a living systematic review that serves as a field-wide reference for measurement choices and effect sizes (Elliott et al., 2017). Because most of the heterogeneity lay between articles and new studies continue to appear, such a review should be measurement-focused and allow researchers to flag omitted effect sizes for eligibility assessment and, when eligible, their automatic incorporation into updated estimates. This could help consolidate standards and reduce unexplained heterogeneity in effect sizes. The recommendations below draw on our results and previous research.

The indirect measure has the practical advantage of retaining separate estimates of personal and other risk. This allows researchers to examine whether a comparative difference originates primarily in judgments about the self, the comparison target, or both. Han and Dang (2025), for example, found different associations of personal-and other-risk judgments with cultural tightness and protective behavior. When these component judgments are theoretically relevant, we therefore recommend using an indirect measure and reporting both estimates separately. Because measurement format was associated with the size of the effect, estimates from direct and indirect measures should also not be compared or combined without considering format.

Response scales should provide sufficient differentiation without assuming that more response options necessarily produce less biased estimates. More generally, psychometric research suggests that gains in reliability, validity, and precision diminish once a moderate number of categories is available (Lozano et al., 2008; Preston & Colman, 2000; Simms et al., 2019). An 11-point scale may therefore offer a reasonable compromise between response resolution and usability, which is consistent with the contrast between 11 and 101 options being close to zero in the present analysis. Leung (2011) found greater sensitivity with 11 options, but small differences in reliability and internal structure. For probability judgments, both 11-point and full 0-100 percentage scales have produced broadly comparable measurement properties (De Bresser, 2019). A 101-point probability scale provides finer numerical resolution and allows responses to be expressed as percentages. Neither previous research nor the present comparison establishes that it produces less biased estimates.

Although our results do not favor a particular comparison target, previous research has shown that target specificity (Kulesza et al., 2023), target group size (Price et al., 2006), and familiarity (Helweg-Larsen & Shepperd, 2001; Zakay, 1996) can influence judgments. We therefore recommend aligning the target closely with the research question and discussing potential influences.

With respect to samples, demographic composition should be reported completely and considered when estimates are compared. Cross-national and temporal differences should be interpreted with attention to sampling, pandemic period, restrictions, testing practices, and other contextual factors rather than attributed to culture or vaccination alone.

Measurement choices should be explicitly justified and documented. Open-science practices were uneven in the included articles, with only five of 38 (13%) preregistered, 20 (53%) sharing data, and 14 (37%) sharing analysis code. We therefore also recommend preregistering studies and sharing data and analysis code, which enables syntheses based on individual participant data. Researchers should report the complete item wording, response anchors, number of response options, comparison target, time horizon, scoring procedure, and response distribution, including category proportions and, where informative, the magnitude of responses within categories (see also Flake & Fried, 2020). Interpretations should also distinguish comparative judgments from objective accuracy and state whether conclusions concern group averages, individual differences, or associations with behavior (Shepperd et al., 2013; Weinstein, 1980).

Limitations

Beyond the limitations of the primary studies discussed above, several limitations arise from the scope and analytical decisions of this synthesis.

First, the synthesis concerned COVID-19 infection during the early pandemic.

Restricting the analysis to one event removed between-event variation, but infection risk still differed across countries, periods, and populations. Generalizability to other events remains uncertain. Comparative optimism may be influenced by perceived and actual base rates (Chambers et al., 2003; Rothman et al., 1996), but studies varied in recruitment windows, geographic reference, and judgment time horizons. A single national incidence value would therefore be difficult to compare across studies and would omit changes in case trajectories, restrictions, local exposure, and testing practices. Longitudinal evidence also indicates that comparative optimism changed across phases of the COVID-19 pandemic (Izydorczak et al., 2022; McColl et al., 2022). We therefore did not include an incidence moderator. The 2020-may partly account for both the remaining heterogeneity and the contextual moderator estimates. In particular, the period coefficient does not estimate a vaccination effect.

Interactions with collection period were not modeled, so it remains untested whether moderator effects differ between 2020 and 2021. Relatedly, studies with data collected through December 31, 2021, were eligible, but the latest included sample was recruited on November 30, 2021. The findings cannot establish whether the pooled effect or moderator patterns apply to later pandemic phases, which would call for a synthesis of their own once enough eligible samples are available.

Second, scale length and measurement format were unevenly distributed across articles. No direct measure used 101 options, and the indirect 5-option category contained only two effects in the moderator dataset. Measurement format, scale length, sample, and article context could therefore not be fully separated, and the sparse crossed cells precluded reliable tests of interactions between measurement format and scale length. Treating scale length through adjacent categorical contrasts also limited assessment of alternative functional forms, including nonlinear changes across the number of response options. The additive format and scale coefficients should be interpreted in view of this imbalance, and the analysis cannot identify a universally optimal response format.

Third, the nominal number of effects exceeds the breadth of independent evidence for several comparisons. Articles could contribute multiple studies or countries. The multilevel model represented study and article clustering and crossed nationality effects, but the sampling-variance matrix could not account for unrecognized participant overlap. We could therefore not establish how many unique participants were represented by the summed sample sizes. Inference also depended on the fitted variance structure. Complete-case demographic models represented fewer articles and omitted the indirect 5-option category, so changes between models may reflect changes in the represented evidence as well as covariate adjustment.

Fourth, the additional OpenAlex search may still have missed relevant studies, especially when full text was not indexed or comparative judgments were described without the required terms. Eligibility was also restricted to reports in English or German and to anonymously recruited adults from general populations, so the findings may not apply to clinically selected samples or telephone interviews, and 10 otherwise eligible reports provided no usable data. A living systematic review, as recommended above, would allow such studies to be added later.

Fifth, the quality assessment used a targeted, domain-specific checklist applied at the article level and coded what was reported, so low ratings may reflect incomplete reporting rather than actual practice. Ambiguous cases received the more favorable rating, so shortcomings are, if anything, underestimated, and the ratings were used descriptively and not related to effect sizes.

Sixth, individual participant data were available for 123 of the 135 effects, so the individual-level analyses rest on a subset, and the study-level moderator associations should not be read as individual-level effects.

Finally, the review and analysis were not prospectively preregistered and should therefore be interpreted as exploratory rather than confirmatory (Nosek et al., 2018). The moderator specification and scale contrasts were finalized during revision, and no multiplicity correction was applied. Several coefficients in the primary and secondary models were close to the significance threshold. For context, a Holm correction (Holm, 1979) applied across all eight individual coefficients in the primary moderator model would leave none below .05, including the measurement-format coefficient, which was robust to omitting single articles but not to such a correction. Thus, the results require independent verification, preferably in prospectively specified analyses and across other events.

Conclusion

This meta-analysis confirms that comparative optimism for COVID-19 infection was observed on average. However, its interpretability is constrained by substantial heterogeneity.

The prediction interval extended from comparative pessimism to pronounced optimism, and most of the variation remained unexplained after the moderator analysis. Point estimates are therefore not generalizable across settings, and selection-model analyses suggest that they may modestly overstate the average effect, although the adjusted estimate remained clearly positive. This highlights a critical issue. Despite our attempt to reduce heterogeneity by restricting the synthesis to a single event, substantial measurement effects and persistent heterogeneity still emerged. Direct measures yielded smaller adjusted effects than indirect measures, and this direction held when single articles were omitted, although the directmeasure evidence came from only 13 articles. Only one of 38 articles addressed statistical artifact theory and none fully justified its response scale, so differences between studies cannot be separated from differences in measurement. Most primary studies therefore left known artifacts and measurement influences unexamined.

Taken together, our results raise reasonable doubt about treating comparative optimism as a fixed quantity. The effect exists on average, but its size, and in some settings its direction, varies across articles, countries, and measurement formats. It is also a group-level comparative difference and does not by itself establish that individual judgments are objectively inaccurate. Future work should prioritize transparent, preregistered measurement choices (format, target, scale length), report distributional diagnostics such as the proportion of equal-risk responses, and test the present moderator patterns in prospectively specified analyses of other events. Broad claims about when comparative optimism occurs and what consequences it has should be made only with its heterogeneity and measurement conditions in view.

Full coefficients for the primary, complete-case, and extended demographic models are presented in Table 5; results for the residual-flag-excluded additive and extended demographic models are reported in Supplemental Tables S10-S11.

Extended Demographic Model

For the complete-case comparison, Model 2 refitted the primary model without the 10 effects missing demographic information (124 effects), so that changes due to the restricted sample could be distinguished from those due to the demographic predictors added in Model 3 (Table 5). Direct measures yielded smaller adjusted effects in both the refitted primary model and the demographic extension. The 11-versus-7 response-option contrast was also negative and statistically significant in both models. The joint scale test was significant after excluding effects with missing demographic information (p = .043), but not when mean age and female proportion were added as predictors (p = .132). The collection-period association was positive in all three models. The collectivism estimate was unchanged at the reported precision after excluding incomplete cases; its confidence interval excluded zero only in the model that added the demographic predictors. These secondary analyses use a reduced evidence set and do not supersede the primary model.

A 10-percentage-point higher female proportion was associated with an approximately 0.043 standard-deviation smaller effect, 95% CI [-0.059, -0.027], p < .001. Mean sample age was not clearly associated with effect size, b = 0.0032 per year, p = .165. The femaleproportion coefficient is a between-sample association and should not be interpreted as an individual-level gender effect. In the extended model excluding the four flagged effects, the these patterns differ across populations and measurement formats, remains a question for future studies.

Moderator Findings

A previous synthesis across events found clearer evidence for event-level moderators (Sweldens et al., 2014), and associations with measurement characteristics may be weakened when effects are combined across events. Restricting the present synthesis to a single event allowed measurement characteristics to be examined without this between-event variation.

We examined measurement format, scale length, and comparison target, which previous work suggests may each influence comparative optimism (Harris & Hahn, 2011; Helweg-Larsen & Shepperd, 2001; Otten & van der Pligt, 1996).

In the present study, direct measures yielded smaller effects than indirect measures after adjustment for the other moderators in the additive model. This difference remained negative in all 38 leave-one-article-out analyses, with a p value below .05 in 37 of them. The direction of this finding is inconsistent with the prediction derived from egocentrism theory that direct judgments should produce larger effects. According to this account, a direct comparison prompts respondents to focus on their own risk-relevant characteristics and behaviors while giving little thought to those of others, whereas indirect measures require separate assessments of personal and others' risk (Weinstein & Lachendro, 1982).

However, measurement formats were not randomly assigned and differed in their distribution across response scales, articles, countries, and periods. The response distributions also differed by format. In Table 2, for example, 52.35% of participants in direct 11-option samples reported higher personal risk, compared with 11.87% in indirect 11-option samples.

Previous research likewise suggests that differences between direct and indirect measures may depend on event characteristics. Rose et al. (2011), for example, found that direct judgments were more strongly influenced by event frequency, whereas indirect judgments were more
